Food assistance / 4–6 min

WICFood assistance for women, infants, and children

The federal nutrition program serves eligible low-income pregnant and postpartum women, infants, and children under five.

Yet millions of eligible people do not receive it. Here’s where access breaks down.

By Megan Quigley

Understand WIC ↓

01 / What WIC provides

  • Food benefits
  • ↗Nutrition &
    breastfeeding support
  • +Health care
    referrals
Who qualifies, and what does WIC cover?

WIC is the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children. It helps eligible low-income pregnant and postpartum women, infants, and children under five who have a nutrition-related need.

It provides specific foods, nutrition education, breastfeeding support, and health care referrals. Food packages vary by life stage; they supplement a grocery budget rather than cover every purchase.

The promise is practical: help during pregnancy and the early years. But there is a distance between being eligible, receiving benefits, and getting food home. This story examines that distance.

USDA: what WIC provides ↗

02 / The national gap

5.2 million eligible people
did not receive WIC.

United States · average month in 2023

How is this counted—and is reach improving?

In an average month in 2023, an estimated 11.83 million people qualified for WIC. 6.63 million participated.

About 5.20 million eligible people were outside the program.

A gap, not a count of denials.

The figures do not tell us why each person did not participate. And reach improved: coverage rose from 53.5% in 2022 to 56.1% in 2023.

USDA estimates eligibility using survey and administrative inputs; participation comes from program data. Exact gap: 11,829,215 − 6,631,309 = 5,197,906. CY2023 was the latest eligibility-and-reach release found in the USDA series during this September 2026 review. Later caseload totals alone do not establish coverage.

USDA national estimates ↗

03 / The child-age gap

WIC reaches 82% of eligible infants.
At age four, just 27%.

Children can qualify until their fifth birthday.

What does the age gap tell us?

WIC can support children until their fifth birthday. Yet it reached 82.3% of eligible infants and just 26.9% of eligible four-year-olds in 2023.

Eligibility does not end
when infancy does.

These are separate age groups, not children tracked over time. The chart cannot separate access barriers from changing needs, food packages, or other circumstances.

What makes support harder to start, keep, or use as children grow?

USDA Table 3.1. The published rounded coverage percentages are shown. Eligibility is estimated; these bars are cross-sectional, not longitudinal. The downloadable age data include eligible and participating counts.

Read the accounts and sources

Interviews in New Hampshire and Vermont documented eligibility misconceptions and competing demands. Most participants also described WIC as convenient once connected. Staff described calls and texts to help families stay enrolled. Support can make these hurdles easier to clear.

Interviews took place February–April 2024 in two New England states; study published in 2026. This small qualitative sample is not nationally representative. The quotation and paraphrases are from the participant findings; outreach accounts are from WIC staff. Accounts are not combined into one invented character.

Read the interview study ↗

California shopping rules document product and balance requirements. These accounts and rules establish specific obstacles; they do not quantify how much each one explains the national participation gap.

Sources, products & assumptions

The comparison assumes approved products and sufficient benefits for 1 gallon of milk, 1 dozen eggs, 20 oz whole grains, one peanut-butter container, and $5.88 in produce. Milk uses the single-gallon price, not the multi-buy promotion. Retailer pickup prices illustrate an in-store WIC transaction; no claim of online WIC payment is made.

California excludes brown eggs for cost containment, not nutrition. Product restrictions and shopping inconvenience also appear in published Philadelphia caregiver interviews; those local accounts do not measure national frequency.

California shopping guidance
Read every grocery rule

Low-fat milk: This example uses one gallon of approved 1% milk for a four-year-old. The milk type, container, and remaining milk benefit must match.

Large white eggs: Approved large white eggs can qualify. California permits qualifying cage-free eggs. One dozen is included in these receipts.

Brown eggs: California excludes brown eggs under its April 2026 rules, citing cost containment. Shell color does not change nutrition. This carton is a comparison only; it is not in the receipts.

Whole-wheat bread: This approved 20 oz whole-wheat loaf uses 20 oz of the whole-grain benefit. The product and package size both matter.

Peanut butter: This approved 18 oz jar uses one peanut-butter container benefit. The child must have that option in the issued package.

Apples: This 3 lb bag of fresh apples uses $3.99 of the fruit-and-vegetable balance. Produce uses dollars rather than a set number of apples.

Frozen peas: These plain frozen peas use $1.89 of the produce balance. Added sauces or other ingredients can change whether vegetables qualify.

Dish soap: WIC pays for approved foods, not dish soap. The household pays the full $3.49 in both receipts.

06 / After enrollment

Getting benefits is one hurdle.
Using them is another.

Local research shows that issued food benefits are not always fully used.

What does benefit use tell us—and what doesn’t it?

In a Southern California study, 69.6% of certification periods reached at least 70% redemption of fruit-and-vegetable benefits. For eggs, the figure was 67.1%.

What can we conclude?

  • Receiving benefits and using them are different measures.
  • Lower redemption was linked to later discontinuation. That does not establish cause.
  • Unused benefits alone prove neither a lack of need nor an access failure.

Preferences, needs, shopping conditions, and other differences may matter. These local findings are not a national estimate of waste.

Study of 188,368 Southern California participants, with repeated certification periods. Table 2: produce 254,506 / 365,738 = 69.6%; eggs 244,775 / 364,908 = 67.1%. Discontinuation means no benefit issuance for two months after certification. Continuing eligibility was not established by that outcome. Observational association, not proof that low redemption caused departure.

JAMA Network Open study ↗

07 / Evidence of improvement

Making benefits easier to use
can help more children take part.

A national study of the shift from paper vouchers to electronic cards.

What changed, and how strong is the evidence?

A national study compared states as WIC moved from paper vouchers to electronic cards. Three years after implementation, participation among children ages one to four was 9.12% higher relative to the comparison.

A relative increase—not a 9.12-point rise in coverage. This study is separate from the national 2023 trend.

The process deserves
the scrutiny, too.

Which changes help eligible families receive and use support—and where are they still being missed?

Difference-in-differences analysis using state participation data, October 2014–November 2019. Table 2 compares EBT and non-EBT states. Child estimate: +9.12% (95% CI 3.19–15.39). The design strengthens inference but is not a randomized trial; other state changes may contribute. Electronic cards are an evaluated past reform, not a claim that states still universally use paper.
